C004.subject: remote work for solitary, well-defined tasks
C004.predicate: reduces error rate compared to office work
C004.object: when workers have high intrinsic motivation
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: remote work for solitary, well-defined tasks when workers have high intrinsic motivation]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled experiment comparing error rates of intrinsically motivated workers on solitary, well-defined tasks in remote vs. office settings, using objective performance metrics (e.g., coding accuracy, data entry error rates). — Directly tests the causal claim under controlled conditions, isolating intrinsic motivation and task type, and provides quantitative evidence to confirm or refute the error rate reduction.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of post-2020 studies on remote work productivity, focusing on task type (solitary/well-defined) and worker motivation (self-reported intrinsic motivation), e.g., from journals like Journal of Applied Psychology or Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes. — Synthesizes existing evidence across multiple studies to assess the generalizability and strength of the relationship, addressing the disputed status with higher statistical power.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal field study using wearable sensors and digital trace data (e.g., keystroke logs, error correction rates) from knowledge workers with high intrinsic motivation (measured via validated scales) in remote and office conditions. — Provides ecological validity and captures real-world error patterns over time, controlling for confounding variables like distraction or ergonomics, to test the hypothesis in naturalistic settings.

qualifier.temporal: post-2020, during widespread remote work adoption

C005.subject: remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: remote work solitary, well-defined tasks]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled lab experiment comparing task completion time and error rates for solitary, well-defined tasks (e.g., data entry, coding) in remote vs. co-located settings during 2020-2021, with participants in high-speed internet countries. — Direct empirical test of the hypothesis by isolating the effect of remote work on efficiency for the specified task type, controlling for confounding variables like distractions or home environment.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies (e.g., from organizational psychology or human-computer interaction journals) that examine productivity changes for routine, independent work during the pandemic period in countries with high-speed internet. — Synthesizes available evidence across multiple contexts to assess the robustness and generalizability of the claimed decrease, leveraging existing data without new collection.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model based on attention resource theory and task-switching costs, predicting that remote work reduces efficiency for solitary well-defined tasks due to increased self-regulation demands and lack of ambient oversight. — Provides a mechanistic explanation for the hypothesis, which can be tested against alternative theories (e.g., autonomy-enhancement theory that predicts efficiency gains), helping to refine the causal logic.

qualifier.geographic: in countries with high-speed internet infrastructure

C006.subject: remote work
C006.object: divergent creative tasks (e.g., brainstorming, ideation) more than convergent collaborative tasks (e.g., decision-making, planning)
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: remote work divergent creative tasks (e.g., brainstorming, ideation) more than convergent collaborative tasks (e.g., decision-making, planning)]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled experiment comparing remote vs. co-located teams on divergent (e.g., brainstorming novel ideas) and convergent (e.g., consensus decision-making) tasks, measuring quantity and quality of outputs. — Directly tests the hypothesis by isolating task type and communication medium, providing causal evidence on differential impairment.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on virtual collaboration and creativity, focusing on moderators such as task type (divergent vs. convergent) and communication richness. — Synthesizes available evidence to assess whether the pattern holds across multiple contexts and identifies boundary conditions.

[PATH:empirical] Naturalistic field study using digital trace data (e.g., communication logs, ideation platform usage) from remote teams to correlate communication patterns with creative outcomes in divergent vs. convergent tasks. — Provides ecological validity by observing real-world remote work, capturing spontaneous interactions and their impact on task performance.

qualifier.rationale: Remote work reduces spontaneous idea cross-pollination and real-time nonverbal feedback, which are critical for divergent thinking but less essential for convergent processes that rely on structured deliberation.

C007.subject: remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: remote work collaborative and creative tasks]

[PATH:empirical] A controlled experiment comparing team performance on creative problem-solving tasks (e.g., design thinking sprints) in co-located vs. fully remote settings, measuring output quality and collaboration efficiency. — Directly tests the causal claim by isolating the remote work variable in a realistic task environment, reducing confounding factors like team composition or tool familiarity.

[PATH:literature] Longitudinal meta-analysis of field studies from 2020–2024 on remote collaboration in knowledge-economy sectors, focusing on innovation metrics (e.g., patent filings, new product ideas) and self-reported creativity. — Aggregates existing evidence across contexts to assess generalizability and temporal trends, addressing the disputed status by identifying consistent patterns or moderators (e.g., task type, team size).

[PATH:empirical] Qualitative case studies of distributed teams in creative industries (e.g., software development, marketing) using digital collaboration tools, analyzing communication logs and artifact evolution to trace how remote work affects idea generation and refinement. — Provides mechanistic understanding of how remote work might enhance or hinder collaborative creativity, revealing mediating factors like asynchronous brainstorming or reduced social pressure.

qualifier.temporal: post-2020, during widespread adoption of digital collaboration tools
qualifier.geographic: global, primarily in knowledge-economy sectors with high internet access

C010.subject: remote work
C010.object: explicitly structured collaborative tasks with high task interdependence

qualifier.tension: Remote work may impair informal learning, but when collaboration is deliberately orchestrated with clear protocols and shared digital artifacts, the reduction in distraction and increased focus can enhance task outcomes, reversing the null or negative effects observed in unstructured settings.
